3.2.5.3-f101.accuracy_reason: In the Historia Augusta's Life of Aelius (5.11), Aelius Verus tells his wife, when she complains of his affairs, that 'uxor' is a name of dignity, not of pleasure.

3.2.5.3-f104.accuracy_reason: The phrase comes from Horace, Satires 1.2.35 ('alienas permolere uxores'), where 'permolere' is a crude sexual metaphor.

3.2.5.3-f106.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of John 6:60 reads 'Durus est hic sermo', the disciples' complaint.

3.2.5.3-f110.accuracy_reason: This is the standard Aristotelian and scholastic idea of prime matter: formless potentiality that 'desires' form.

3.2.5.3-f114.accuracy_reason: 'Conjurgium' is the well-known pun that puts 'jurgium' (quarrel) inside 'conjugium' (marriage).

3.2.5.3-f115.accuracy_reason: Semonides fr. 7, lines 99–100, says that a man who lives with a woman never passes a whole day cheerful. Burton's sidenote names Semonides.

3.2.5.3-f120.accuracy_reason: In Suetonius, Augustus 65, Augustus quotes in Greek an adaptation of Iliad 3.40, Hector's rebuke to Paris, wishing he had lived unwed and died childless.

3.2.5.3-f121.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Augustus 65, has Augustus call the two Julias and Agrippa Postumus his 'three boils and three cancers' (tris vomicas ac tria carcinomata).

3.2.5.3-f122.accuracy_reason: The remark is in the Historia Augusta, Life of Severus 20, attributed to Spartianus.

3.2.5.3-f124.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 6.167–8 ('malo, malo Venustinam quam te, Cornelia, mater Gracchorum'), the speaker prefers a simple girl to the haughty, virtuous Cornelia. Burton's use of it for the over-accomplished wife fits the passage that follows.

3.2.5.3-f132.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.460 reads 'intolerabilius nihil est quam femina dives', and the note shows Burton's recasting correctly.

3.2.5.3-f139.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 1.26 tells how Thales, urged by his mother to marry, said it was not yet time and later that the time had passed. This fits Burton's lines just before the phrase.

3.2.5.3-f14.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.288–289 reads 'Mnesthea Sergestumque vocat fortemque Serestum, / classem aptent taciti sociosque ad litora cogant'. The note reports Burton's changes correctly.

3.2.5.3-f142.accuracy_reason: The full line is 'cum castum amisit polluto corpore florem', so Burton breaks off before 'polluto corpore florem', not 'just before florem'. Burton also drops 'est' after 'suis', which the note doesn't mention. The rest is right: Catullus 62, and the readings convulsus and quem.

3.2.5.3-f145.accuracy_reason: Martial 12.34 ends 'nulli te facias nimis sodalem: / gaudebis minus et minus dolebis', which is second person as the note says.

3.2.5.3-f15.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.438–439 reads 'nullis ille movetur / fletibus aut voces ullas tractabilis audit', on Aeneas unmoved by Dido.

3.2.5.3-f158.accuracy_reason: The word is clearly formed from Xanthippe, and Burton glosses it as 'a shrew to my wife'.

3.2.5.3-f176.accuracy_reason: Suetonius (Iul. 52.3) does not present the law as a rumour. He says the tribune Helvius Cinna told many people he had the bill drafted and ready to propose on Caesar's orders. Burton's 'others suspect it' refers to commentators such as Torrentius.

3.2.5.3-f177.accuracy_reason: Suetonius has 'uti uxores liberorum quaerendorum causa quas et quot vellet ducere liceret', which the note's hedged 'roughly' fairly covers. The point that Burton generalises the law to great men is right.

3.2.5.3-f189.accuracy_reason: Andria 254–255 reads 'uxor tibi ducendast, Pamphile, hodie… abi domum. id mihi visust dicere "abi cito ac suspende te"', as the note says.

3.2.5.3-f201.accuracy_reason: Plautus, Asinaria 87, reads 'argentum accepi, dote imperium vendidi', and Burton does attach the line to his Seneca citation.

3.2.5.3-f202.accuracy_reason: 'Nubere' is used of the bride, and the joke works as the note describes. The line is Martial 8.12, though the note doesn't name it.

3.2.5.3-f206.accuracy_reason: 'Idiota' is the accepted pen name of Raymundus Jordanus, who wrote the Contemplationes de amore divino.

3.2.5.3-f207.accuracy_reason: The 'Tom. 2 in votis' citation points to Lucian's Navigium (Vota), where Lycinus and Timolaus are speakers. 'Simus' means snub-nosed, and Burton's English does say 'crook-nosed'.

3.2.5.3-f209.accuracy_reason: Joseph Hall published Mundus alter et idem under the name Mercurius Britannicus, and Viraginia is its land of women.

3.2.5.3-f217.accuracy_reason: The lines are Parmeno's in Terence's Eunuchus, 1.1 (lines 57–58).

3.2.5.3-f24.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.3.19–20, has the crow (cornicula) 'furtivis nudata coloribus'. Burton changes it to the accusative.

3.2.5.3-f32.accuracy_reason: Martial 3.89.2 reads 'nam faciem durum, Phoebe, cacantis habes'. Burton leaves out 'durum' and turns the line on a woman.

3.2.5.3-f36.accuracy_reason: Cicero, In Catilinam 1.10, reads 'Patent portae; proficiscere', and 'profiscere' is a corrupt spelling of it.

3.2.5.3-f46.accuracy_reason: The line is from the chorus on the transience of beauty in Seneca's Phaedra (around line 773).

3.2.5.3-f47.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.113, reads 'forma bonum fragile est'.

3.2.5.3-f48.accuracy_reason: The lines are Phaedra 761–762, in the same chorus, and Hippolytus is the play's other title.

3.2.5.3-f53.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.297–298 reads 'rara est adeo concordia formae / atque pudicitiae'.

3.2.5.3-f56.accuracy_reason: Rufinus, Greek Anthology 5.94, gives Melite Hera's eyes, Athena's hands, Aphrodite's breasts and Thetis' ankles. Saying that 'Idem' points to the preceding note's author is the normal meaning.

3.2.5.3-f69.accuracy_reason: Thucydides 2.45: Pericles says a woman's greatest glory is to be least talked of among men, whether for praise or blame.

3.2.5.3-f77.accuracy_reason: Anteros is correctly described as the god of returned love, or the avenger of slighted love.

3.2.5.3-f78.accuracy_reason: In Satires 1.2.54 the words are not Horace's own boast of restraint. They are the self-praise of a profligate (Sallustius), whom Horace mocks for ruining himself on freedwomen. The rest of the note is right.

3.2.5.3-f80.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.69–70, is correctly quoted and glossed.

3.2.5.3-f81.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus (13.559) quotes this Menander fragment on marriage as a sea of troubles.

3.2.5.3-f86.accuracy_reason: The lines come from Seneca's Hercules Oetaeus, in the speech about Deianira's jealous rage.

3.2.5.3-f89.accuracy_reason: Semonides fr. 7 calls women the greatest evil Zeus made. The note rightly calls the Latin a paraphrase, not a quotation.

3.2.5.3-f93.accuracy_reason: Tyrotarichum (a dish of cheese and salt fish) appears in Cicero's letters to Atticus as a cheap, simple meal.

3.2.5.3-f95.accuracy_reason: Athenaeus book 13 preserves this comic fragment, which the sidenote attributes to Eubulus.

3.2.5.3-f96.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 6.43 does read 'stulta maritali iam porrigit ora capistro', and Burton's change from 'iam' to 'qui' is described correctly.
